newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood attacks Afghan Taleban in rear-line town.
newsitem.headline: Masood attacks Afghan Taleban in rear-line town.

text.p: The forces of ousted Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood hit the Islamic Taleban militia in a town behind the front lines on Saturday, putting scores of the black-turbanned warriors to flight.

But the Taleban appeared to have quelled what they called an insurgency in villages farther south, some 15 km (10 miles) north of the capital Kabul. Pick-up trucks loaded with fighters were seen heading north out of Kabul on Saturday afternoon.
Masood forces fired about 300 shells and mortar bombs into Kabul's main airbase 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul overnight.
The Taleban responded with bombing raids, witnesses said.
They said two MiG-21s bombed the village of Bagram next to the airbase, apparently aiming at Masood positions, but it was not clear what damage had been done to them or in the overnight shelling.

Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces and local commanders who apparently turned against the Taleban just two weeks after the mainly Pushtun movement took Kabul, attacked at several points on Friday and cut the main road north to the front lines.

Taleban in positions a few km (miles) north of the capital who had been firing rockets into positions west of the road on Friday said they had crushed the attack and pointed to smoking buildings in the distance, which they said were the houses of the commanders behind the attacks.
They said the road was clear, but round the next corner the situation was more tense.
Taleban fighters crowding around a dozen pickups and military vehicles across the road angrily ordered a car of journalists to turn back.
"Listen clearly. If I see you people again I will rape you and then kill you," one said. It was not clear whether the Taleban were in control of the highway ahead or not.

Earlier on Saturday, Masood struck at Charikar, a mainly Tajik town a 30-minute drive from the Taleban front line headquarters at Jabal-os-Saraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains which divide Afghanistan.
At a Taleban roadblock just south of Charikar, the sound of heavy automatic rifle fire echoed around the town.

Suddenly a convoy of Taleban trucks and pick-ups, along with a mobile rocket launcher truck, drove towards the road block at high speed, trailing a huge cloud of dust that obscured the sight of winter's first snow on the mountain tops.
Taleban fighters at the checkpoint raised a chain across the road in an apparent attempt to stop them heading towards Kabul.
The convoy slewed around the chain and stopped briefly to ask journalists whether the road to Kabul was open.
As they began to move off, a Taleban guard at the roadblock walked towards the mobile rocket launcher and fired a shot towards it in what appeared to be an effort to halt the flight.
The convoy took off again at high speed in another huge cloud of dust and the guard fired another shot after it.
The roadblock guards refused to talk about the fighting that appeared to be going on in Charikar, brusquely ordering journalists to leave.
Further south, the main road to Kabul remained closed and even the Taleban convoy had to take a looping side road to the capital that runs past the Bagram air base.
Witnesses said a 20-km (12-mile) strech of road starting about 15 km (nine miles) north of Kabul remained closed with fighting still going on in the area.
Near Bagram, witnesses said they had seen two warplanes swoop in from the south and drop bombs on Bagram village, whose people fled on Thursday fearing imminent battles.
Winnesses in Kabul reported two jets taking off from there shortly beforehand and an hour later another warplane took off from Kabul airport and headed north.
People around Bagram, where the population is largely Tajik, said Masood's fighters had infiltrated the area.

In Kabul, acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi dismissed what Afghan watchers in the capital called the worst military reverses the Taleban had suffered since the movement was launched in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago.
"Our operation in the north of Kabul is against bandits and those forces which destroyed Afghanistan, looted the treasury and defamed Jihad (Holy War) and Islam," he told Reuters.
